title: Search, indexes & vector retrieval
summary: Understand lexical search, embeddings, approximate indexes, and ranking before adding an LLM.
html:
Understand lexical search, embeddings, approximate indexes, and ranking before adding an LLM.

How the pieces connect

Ingest → Index → Retrieve → Verify. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it.

Lexical and semantic retrieval

An inverted index maps terms to matching documents. BM25 uses term frequency, document length, and term rarity for lexical ranking. Dense retrieval maps queries and documents to embeddings and compares them with an appropriate similarity measure. Lexical search is strong for exact identifiers; dense search can recover paraphrases.

Approximate nearest neighbors

Exact vector search scans all candidates and can be expensive. HNSW navigates a graph; IVF partitions vector space; product quantization compresses representations. Index settings trade recall, latency, build cost, and memory. Evaluate retrieval recall against exact search on a representative sample.

Chunking defines what can be retrieved

A chunk should preserve enough context to answer a question while remaining focused. Respect headings, tables, code boundaries, and source metadata. Overlap can reduce boundary losses but duplicates content and increases index size. Track document versions and delete stale chunks.

Rerank and authorize

A reranker spends more computation on a small candidate set. Hybrid retrieval can merge lexical and semantic evidence. Enforce access permissions before exposing retrieved content and check them again if documents change. A citation must point to a source passage that actually supports the answer.

Worked example

For “error E1042 in firmware 2.7,” lexical matching preserves the exact code and version. For “why does the device restart after sleeping,” embeddings may find a differently worded power-management note. A hybrid candidate set plus a reranker can combine both strengths.

What goes wrong

Nearest in embedding space does not mean true, relevant, current, or authorized. An LLM cannot answer from a passage retrieval never found.

Check your understanding

What should you measure before answer quality in RAG?

Reveal the explanation

Whether the required evidence appears in the retrieved top-k results, then whether the generated answer is supported by that evidence.

An operating model for search, indexes & vector retrieval

Retrieval quality places a hard ceiling on grounded generation. If the source passage is absent from the candidate set, a later reranker or language model cannot reliably recover it. Treat retrieval recall, source freshness, and authorization as first-class product metrics before prompt polish.

The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test.

Worked system: the answer cannot outrun retrieval recall

A maintenance assistant receives the question “Why does firmware 2.7 restart after sleep?” If the candidate set omits the power-management bulletin, a language model may write a plausible answer but it cannot ground it in the required evidence. Retrieval is therefore a two-stage problem: first find a set that contains the answer; then rank, quote, and synthesize it. Generation quality should be measured only after evidence recall is known.

Construct a small benchmark where each question names the required passage or passages. Inspect exact-code queries separately from paraphrases, stale documents separately from current ones, and unauthorized documents separately from authorized ones. A nearest neighbor is merely a geometric neighbor; it is not automatically true, current, or permitted.

Notebook: Make the split an explicit artifact

Maintain a query set with required passages and unanswerable cases. Measure top-k evidence recall, citation entailment, latency, and access-control behavior separately.

train_ids = set(train["record_id"])
assert not train_ids & set(test["record_id"])
assert train["event_time"].max() <= cutoff
# Fit transformations only after this boundary exists.
What to test next. 1. Ingest: Parse, normalize, version, and authorize documents. 2. Index: Build lexical and vector representations. 3. Retrieve: Generate a candidate set for the query. 4. Verify: Rerank, cite, and abstain when evidence is absent.

The gotcha. A small inspection script proves only the quantities it prints. Preserve units, shapes, versions, and the input fixture beside its output.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Ingest. Parse, normalize, version, and authorize documents.
  2. Index. Build lexical and vector representations.
  3. Retrieve. Generate a candidate set for the query.
  4. Verify. Rerank, cite, and abstain when evidence is absent.

Maintain a query set with required passages and unanswerable cases. Measure top-k evidence recall, citation entailment, latency, and access-control behavior separately.
